---
title: "Design Lab: A Deterministic Stock Exchange Simulator"
---

# Design Lab: A Deterministic Stock Exchange Simulator

Build a Go matching-engine simulator for one synthetic symbol. The engineering problem is deterministic ordering and recovery. Use fixed integer ticks for prices and integer lots for quantities; define units and validate overflow before accepting orders.

## Specify matching rules

Support limit orders and cancellation. The best bid is the highest price; the best ask is the lowest. Within a price level, use FIFO acceptance order. An incoming buy crosses asks at or below its limit, and an incoming sell crosses bids at or above its limit. In this lab, executions use the resting order's price.

Store bids and asks as ordered price levels with FIFO queues, and keep an order-ID index for cancellation. A heap of price levels plus per-level queues is enough for the small baseline; cancellation requires removing or marking an indexed order without corrupting its queue.

## Sequence before matching

Route every accepted command for the symbol through one bounded sequencer. Assign a monotonic sequence number and append a framed command to a durable log under a stated sync policy. Only then apply it to the single-owner matching engine and publish executions with IDs derived from sequence and fill index.

A Go command model can be:

```go
type Command struct {
	RequestID, OrderID string
	Kind, Side         string
	PriceTicks, Lots   int64
}

type Execution struct {
	Sequence            uint64
	FillIndex           uint32
	BuyOrder, SellOrder string
	PriceTicks, Lots    int64
}
```

These are model fragments, not a complete exchange. Duplicate request IDs must return the original acceptance/result and reject conflicting payloads. HTTP arrival time and goroutine scheduling are not the authoritative order; the assigned sequence is.

Create snapshots with their applied sequence. Recovery loads a snapshot and replays later logged commands, producing exactly the same book and execution IDs. A crash after logging but before response can leave a command accepted from the engine's perspective; the retry/status contract resolves it by request ID.

## Risk and distribution boundaries

Before acceptance, a risk component reserves synthetic cash or inventory. Matching, reservation release, and settlement need explicit recovery states; do not claim two independent services commit atomically. For the first milestone keep risk and matching state in the same deterministic simulation.

Partition by symbol for independent matching. Only one fenced leader may sequence a symbol at a time. Broadcasting the same order to two active engines creates contradictory fills. Market-data subscribers receive sequence numbers and recover gaps through snapshots/replay, with bounded outbound queues.

## Acceptance evidence

Rest asks for 5 lots at 100 and 4 lots at 101, then buy 7 lots with limit 101. Expect fills of 5 at 100 and 2 at 101, leaving 2 at 101. Add equal-price FIFO tests, cancel-versus-fill ordering, partial fills, duplicate submissions, and an over-capacity admission rejection.

Kill after log append and before apply; recover and compare a deterministic state hash and execution list against uninterrupted replay. Measure sequencer queue age, acceptance latency, replay time, and subscriber gap recovery. Describe this as a simulator of the declared rules, not a model of every real venue's order types or operating obligations.
